`charport` defines a boundary between packages that produce ALTREP strings and
packages that consume them. This document describes the guarantees at that
boundary and which package owns each responsibility.

## What `charport` does not do

`charport` is not a string API. It does not define matching, collation,
normalization, locale behavior, recycling rules, or missing-value policy beyond
representing a missing string view.

It also does not try to own every ALTREP string representation. Existing
packages can keep their storage layout, construction path, and user-facing
semantics. `charport` only gives those packages a way to answer read requests
with byte views when doing so is safe.

## Why the contract is narrow

The interface exposes byte views, reader capabilities, and lifetime rules.
ALTREP producers do not need to adopt another storage model, and consumers do
not need class-specific code. If a vector cannot satisfy the direct-read
contract, `charport::Reader` falls back to ordinary R character-vector access.

## Plain data at the boundary

The public boundary is a C ABI made from plain data: function pointers,
booleans, lengths, `SEXP`, and small structs such as `charport_strview`,
`charport_byteview`, and `charport_reader`.

This avoids binding downstream packages to a C++ object layout, exception
model, or framework dependency. C++ users still get a wrapper API in
`charport.h`, while the package boundary remains plain C data.

## Borrowed views and materialization

A `charport::Reader` is an active borrow of a character vector's current string
storage. During that borrow, code should avoid accessing or modifying the same
R object through other R APIs, because ALTREP methods may materialize, cache,
or replace internal storage.

The strict borrow follows from the ALTREP contract: another ALTREP class may
materialize, cache, or replace its internal storage during ordinary R access.
Direct views remain valid under the reader contract, and ordinary R access is
the fallback when that contract is unavailable.

## Reader capabilities and diagnostics

`Reader::persistent_views()` means returned byte pointers remain valid for the
lifetime of the `Reader`, even after later reader access. This supports
patterns such as collecting views on the main thread and processing those views
later while the borrow is active.

`Reader::concurrent_access()` means reader access calls may be made from worker
threads and from multiple threads at once. `Reader::reentrant()` is a
convenience check that returns true only when both guarantees are true.

The primary read path is block access: consumers ask for ranges or indexed
selections of byte views, lengths, or encodings. Scalar access remains
available for element-wise code, while block access avoids a callback for each
element.

For diagnostics, `charport::sexp_info(x)` and `charport_info(x)` inspect a
vector without forcing it. They report whether the object is a character
vector, whether it is ALTREP, whether ordinary string pointer storage is
already available, whether a registered ALTREP class matches, the reader
capability flags, and whether a registered reader would own per-reader state.

These helpers are for development, debugging, and preflight checks. Ordinary
read logic constructs a `Reader` and uses its reported capabilities. The C ABI
reports ALTREP class and package names as borrowed `const char *` pointers so
the diagnostic struct remains plain C data.

## Errors and unwinding

`charport` crosses package boundaries. At those boundaries, the common error
mechanism is R's condition system, not a particular C++ exception type.

Registered callbacks and `.Call` entry points must not let C++ exceptions
return through a C ABI or R API boundary. If C++ code can throw, catch the
exception inside the package that owns that code and convert it to an R error,
a `NULL` reader init result, or another explicit status.

R errors can long-jump. Code that calls R APIs must account for that behavior,
especially around ownership transfer and cleanup.

## Encoding policy

`charport` carries encoding marks, but it does not translate, normalize, or
reinterpret strings. `StrView` reports bytes, length, and an encoding mark;
`ByteView`, `length()`, and `encoding()` expose smaller pieces of the same
low-level contract. Block access uses caller-owned pointer, length, and
encoding arrays so consumers can work without allocating one wrapper object per
element.

Packages that need normalization or locale-aware behavior implement that policy
above the byte-view layer.

## C++11 and framework independence

`charport` is intended to be a low-level dependency for other packages.
Requiring Rcpp, cpp11, or another C++ framework would make that dependency
heavier and would force a framework choice on packages that may already have
one.

The installed header therefore uses ordinary C and C++11. Packages that use
Rcpp or cpp11 can still integrate naturally through their init hooks and
compiled code, but `charport` itself does not require them.
